title: Saint-Gobain's researchers, Microsoft’s engineers: One team tackling a decades-old challenge - Source
body_markdown:
Mojdeh Rastgoo-Lemaitre is a French-Iranian computer engineer working in research at the global construction materials giant[Saint-Gobain](https://www.saint-gobain.com/en/look-around) . Ossi Ottka is a Finnish computer engineer with[Microsoft Frontier Company](https://www.microsoft.com/en-us/frontier-company) , helping businesses find solutions to their biggest business and technical problems.


Together, with a combined team of engineers and scientists from both companies, they tackled a problem that Saint-Gobain had been pursuing for more than two decades in a matter of months — finding new molecules that could be used in an additive to make a lower-carbon cement.


“We could see that, around the table, everybody has a Ph.D. and everybody knows something,” recalls Rastgoo-Lemaitre, a digital acceleration program manager at Saint-Gobain. “But everyone was humble about what they know and don’t know, and everyone was very open to learn.”


Engineers from the Microsoft Frontier Company learned a little about Saint-Gobain and the chemistry behind making cement, which is the binding element in concrete. And the Saint-Gobain engineers learned a little about Microsoft and software. “We were all working as one team,” says Rastgoo-Lemaitre. “That was, I think, the reason for success.”


Cutting-edge agentic AI technology was involved, but when both looked back on the successful collaboration, they came to a similar conclusion: The process that led to the breakthrough was as important as the tools they used to get there.


“We started working in two-week sprints,” says Rastgoo-Lemaitre, “and we learned a lot from the Microsoft team how to actually work in this manner. And the expertise of the team, obviously the software engineering skills were highly appreciated.”


## **Finding new answers to old questions**


The collaboration began about two years ago, when a team of “forward-deployed engineers” (or FDEs) from Microsoft began working with the research teams at Saint-Gobain on improving the formula for a cement additive that could maintain or strengthen the resulting concrete while lowering CO2 emissions. In this phase, the effort was made using the same ingredients in the formula that existed then. That success left both sides enthusiastic about further collaboration.


The question was: What’s next?


“We always approach this from business value and try to ask the customer, ‘what’s your most important problem, your most important challenge? What could have the biggest ROI \[return on investment\] for you?’” says Ottka, a development lead on the collaboration with Saint-Gobain who also had worked on the earlier project.


Rastgoo-Lemaitre says that leaders from Saint-Gobain’s product group saw greater potential in a chemistry breakthrough — discovering a new molecule that could improve the cement additive’s performance — than in the earlier improvements to the existing formula. They explained that such a breakthrough could lead to a more value-added product and greater reductions in CO2 emissions.


At about the same time this spring, Microsoft was ready to share its[Microsoft Discovery](https://azure.microsoft.com/en-us/solutions/discovery) platform in private review. Saint-Gobain’s cement additive mission was seen as a good match.


The merged team of engineers worked on testing and improving the Discovery platform while investigating the best way to conduct the research.[In brief](https://news.microsoft.com/source/emea/features/a-concrete-vision-saint-gobain-and-microsoft-discovery-build-for-the-future/) , using Microsoft Discovery, the group created a knowledge base that extended far beyond traditional parameters when it comes to cement chemistry.


“We actually gathered 62,000 patents and 44,000 abstracts,” says Rastgoo-Lemaitre. “Without using this technology, it would have taken our researchers a year to create the knowledge base. Using AI, it took us a couple of hours.” Within weeks afterward this past summer, the group had found several potential new molecules and hypotheses for new formulas.


## **Building trust, one step at a time**


Ottka says, “the tricky thing with Frontier R&D is that, in order to get really good results, you do need access to essentially the most important data of a company — and companies are often rightfully very cautious about access to this data.” Security is front and center in the Microsoft Frontier Company approach, Ottka says. Saint-Gobain’s data, Intellectual Property (IP) and competitive advantage stay protected and in the control of the company.


## “Saint-Gobain’s team challenged us a lot on security,”


— Ossi Ottka is an AI software engineer and development lead for Microsoft Frontier Company; he spent two years working with researchers at the construction materials giant Saint-Gobain.


“They had a very mature process for assessing the security of the new platform. And they challenged us a lot on some of the building blocks.”


The skills and expertise of the Saint-Gobain team, he says, helped identify ways to improve features in Discovery, including a fix that helped reduce the cost of running a part of the system.


Ehsan Zare Borzeshi was among the first Microsoft FDE leaders to engage with Saint-Gobain on the cement projects, and he is now part of the Microsoft Frontier Company as Global FDE lead for Frontier R&D.


He described the Microsoft Frontier Company approach as bringing research and development into the flow of business, using AI tools of various sorts to accelerate the scientific discovery and/or process to deliver business impact. But he emphasized that the process is more important than which technology is used.


“Our goal is solving the most impactful problem for you — not bringing product into the picture, not bringing technology into the picture,” Zare Borzeshi says.


Rastgoo-Lemaitre appreciated the humility of the Microsoft team, she says. That led to a sense of trust and togetherness that left a lasting mark.


“The Microsoft team took the necessary time to share their knowledge and expertise and took us through every step of the way,” she says.


“We all felt that we were part of one team.… I can tell you that it’s not the case with any external partner. So we had a great time working with them.”
